RagShortTexts: The House of Wittelsbach held Bavaria and the Palatinate under the iconic blue-and-white.

Variants.Content: The Wittelsbach held Bavaria and the Rhenish Palatinate under the blue-and-white lozenges of their arms. In 1255 the family divided its lands between Louis II and Henry XIII, creating an Upper Bavarian and Palatine line and a Lower Bavarian line that governed separately. The Palatine branch also held the dignity of Count Palatine of the Rhine, which carried a vote in imperial elections and made the Wittelsbach a power in the Empire's politics. The dukes kept Bavaria's rivers and Alpine passes under their control, and their tolls and salt revenues paid for castles and retinues. Through the division the family learned to balance imperial service against its own territorial needs, and that balance shaped every decision about alliances and inheritance.

Duke Louis the Strict kept his castles on the Alpine passes and his tolls on the Rhine in good repair, and he sent his bailiffs to every market where salt and grain changed hands. Each toll was entered in the ducal rolls, and every new alliance with a rival archbishop was weighed against the cost of raids on those routes.
Bavarian farms brew rich barley beer under customary land law. So long as dues in smoked hams and oats are delivered to ducal bailiffs, the valleys enjoy peace.
